newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Bhutto husband says he fears police will poison him.
newsitem.headline: Bhutto husband says he fears police will poison him.

text.p: Ousted Pakistani prime minister Benazir Bhutto's detained husband Asif Ali Zardari told a court on Saturday that police were harrassing him and that he feared they would try to poison him.
"They (police) are not allowing me to sleep and I fear they are going to poison me," he told a judicial magistrate when brought before her by the police.

Zardari was re-arrested on Thursday on suspicion of involvement in the alleged murder of his wife's estranged brother Murtaza Bhutto as soon as he was released from a Karachi jail after a court declared his six-week detention illegal.
The magistrate, Rashida Siddiqui, refused a police request for a 14-day custody order for Zardari's interrogation, saying the police had not prepared a proper case against the accused.
She said that unless police produced all relevant documents within 24 hours, Zardari would be returned to judicial custody -- where police would not be permitted to question him.
Zardari told the magistrate he had been falsely implicated in the murder of someone he had always respected.
"It is only due to President (Farooq) Leghari's personal enmity. How could I murder a person I had always respected and had never even said anything against him," Zardari said.
Mumtaz Ali Bhutto, the chief minister of Sindh province, of which Karachi is the capital, said on Friday more loyalists of Benazir Bhutto might be arrested for allegedly conspiring to murder Murtaza.
Police say Murtaza was killed in a crossfire after his bodyguards fired first at police.
A judicial tribunal is already investigating the incident, which Benazir says was a conspiracy against her family and government, which was sacked on November 5 by President Leghari.
Bhutto and Zardari have been at the centre of corruption allegations associated with the former government. Both deny any wrongdoing.

Bhutto and Murtaza had developed differences over rival claims to the leadership of the party founded by their father, former prime minister Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, who was toppled in an army coup in 1977 and hanged in 1979 after a controversial conviction for a murder conspiracy.
Murtaza returned from 16 years in exile in 1993 and last year set up his breakaway version of the Pakistan People's Party.
